# Appendix A: Evaluating the example with the interval score {- #appendix-a}

This appendix repeats the worked example of [the example section](#example), using the interval score as the metric for comparison rather than the empirical coverage. For a central $1 - \alpha$ prediction interval $[l, u]$ and an observed outcome $y$ the interval score is defined as:

$$
S_\alpha(l, u; y) = (u - l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l - y)\,\mathbf{1}\{y < l\} + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y - u)\,\mathbf{1}\{y > u\}
$$

The interval score is a proper scoring rule that rewards narrow intervals while penalizing intervals that fail to contain the outcome. Lower values indicate sharper, better-calibrated intervals. The calibration and test sets, the estimated random forest model, and every `pinterval_*()` call are identical to the main text. The only change in the replication code is the evaluation step which uses `interval_score()` rather than `interval_coverage()`. Because the interval score trades the width of the intervals against miscoverage, we also report the mean interval width of each method, computed with `interval_width()`.

We begin with the standard conformal, normal parametric, and bootstrapped intervals.

```{r score-scp-norm-boot}
conformal_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = conformal_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = conformal_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

norm_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = norm_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = norm_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

bootstrap_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = bootstrap_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = bootstrap_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

c(conformal_score, norm_score, bootstrap_score)
```

```{r width-scp-norm-boot}
conformal_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = conformal_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = conformal_intervals$upper_bound
)

norm_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = norm_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = norm_intervals$upper_bound
)

bootstrap_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = bootstrap_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = bootstrap_intervals$upper_bound
)

c(conformal_width, norm_width, bootstrap_width)
```

The three methods produce almost identical aggregate interval scores. This is not surprising, given the small difference in coverage rates noted in the main text. The mean interval widths are similarly close, ranging from 0.301 for the bootstrapped intervals to 0.304 for the normal parametric intervals.

We next score the MCP, CCP, and DWCP intervals.

```{r score-mcp-ccp-dwcp}
mondrian_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = mondrian_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = mondrian_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

clustered_conformal_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = clustered_conformal_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = clustered_conformal_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

distance_weighted_cp_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = distance_weighted_cp_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = distance_weighted_cp_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

c(mondrian_score, clustered_conformal_score,
  distance_weighted_cp_score)
```

```{r width-mcp-ccp-dwcp}
mondrian_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = mondrian_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = mondrian_intervals$upper_bound
)

clustered_conformal_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = clustered_conformal_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = clustered_conformal_intervals$upper_bound
)

distance_weighted_cp_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = distance_weighted_cp_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = distance_weighted_cp_intervals$upper_bound
)

c(mondrian_width, clustered_conformal_width,
  distance_weighted_cp_width)
```

Here too we see that the overall interval scores are similar, with a slightly lower (better) score for the CCP algorithm. As the CCP intervals are, on average, marginally wider than the MCP and DWCP intervals, the lower score of the CCP algorithm stems from smaller penalties for miscoverage rather than from sharper intervals.

To obtain the interval score within each US Census region, we reuse the combined tibble `all_conformal_intervals` assembled in the main text and summarize with `interval_score()` and `interval_width()`.

```{r group-wise-score}
group_wise_score <- all_conformal_intervals %>%
  group_by(method, region) %>%
  summarise(
    score = interval_score(
      truth = rel_dem_share,
      lower_bound = lower_bound,
      upper_bound = upper_bound,
      alpha = 0.1
    ),
    width = interval_width(
      lower_bound = lower_bound,
      upper_bound = upper_bound
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

group_wise_score %>%
  group_by(method) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_score = mean(score),
    mean_width = mean(width)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-width) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = region,
    values_from = score
  )
```

The results clearly show that the CCP and MCP algorithms produce lower mean interval scores when aggregating across the US Census regions. The mean interval widths, in contrast, differ little between the methods, ranging from 0.301 to 0.311. The improvement of the group-aware algorithms therefore does not come from narrower intervals, but from adapting the intervals to each region.

Finally, we score the bin-conditional conformal intervals, both in aggregate and within each range of the outcome.

```{r score-bccp}
bccp_contiguized_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  lower_bound = bccp_contiguized_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = bccp_contiguized_intervals$upper_bound,
  alpha = 0.1
)

bccp_discontigous_score <- interval_score(
  truth = test$rel_dem_share,
  intervals = bccp_discontigous_intervals$intervals,
  alpha = 0.1
)

c(bccp_contiguized_score, bccp_discontigous_score)
```

```{r width-bccp}
bccp_contiguized_width <- interval_width(
  lower_bound = bccp_contiguized_intervals$lower_bound,
  upper_bound = bccp_contiguized_intervals$upper_bound
)

bccp_discontigous_width <- interval_width(
  intervals = bccp_discontigous_intervals$intervals
)

c(bccp_contiguized_width, bccp_discontigous_width)
```

Both BCCP variants produce wider intervals than the other methods, with the discontiguous version being narrower than the contiguized one since it can exclude the gaps between non-adjacent bins from the prediction set.

```{r bin-wise-score}
bin_wise_score <- all_intervals_bins %>%
  group_by(method, truth_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    score = interval_score(
      truth = rel_dem_share,
      lower_bound = lower_bound,
      upper_bound = upper_bound,
      intervals = intervals,
      alpha = 0.1
    ),
    width = interval_width(
      lower_bound = lower_bound,
      upper_bound = upper_bound,
      intervals = intervals
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bin_wise_score %>%
  group_by(method) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_score = mean(score),
    mean_width = mean(width)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-width) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = truth_bin,
    values_from = score
  )
```

The results indicate that the BCCP algorithm does not produce lower interval scores on average compared to the alternative methods. However, looking closely at the results, the BCCP algorithms seem to have an edge over the competing algorithms in both bin 1 and bin 4, and perform worse than the competing algorithms in bins 2 and 3. This is in line with expectations given how the interval score trades the interval width versus the miscoverage. As can be seen in the results for coverage, methods not taking the ranges of the prediction target into account tend to over-cover the middle of the distribution and under-cover the tails (i.e., bins 1 and 4). The BCCP algorithm achieves this by widening the prediction intervals, with mean interval widths of 0.321 and 0.310 for the contiguized and discontiguous versions, compared with 0.301 to 0.304 for the other methods. This leads to a higher interval score in the regions where other algorithms have narrower, over-covering, intervals. Conversely, because the BCCP algorithm achieves near the nominal coverage rate in bins 1 and 4, the interval score for these bins are lower for the BCCP methods. These results are further confirmed by the simulation study in [Appendix B](#appendix-b) below.

# Appendix B: Simulation-based evaluation of prediction interval methods {- #appendix-b}

This appendix presents a simulation study designed to systematically evaluate the empirical coverage properties of the prediction interval methods implemented in the **pintervals** package. While the main text illustrates these methods using a single train-calibration-test split, mimicking a real-world forecasting scenario, the simulation study assesses their performance across repeated random splits of the calibration and test data. Crucially, the training data remains constant throughout the simulation, only the calibration and test data are re-assigned by merging these two partitions and then splitting them into 50/50 calibration and test partitions. In total, we run 1000 simulations.

Across all simulation settings, the target coverage level is fixed at $1 - \alpha = 0.9$. For each simulation, prediction intervals are constructed using the same procedures described in the main text, and performance is summarized using (i) empirical coverage, i.e., the proportion of observations in the test set whose true value is within the corresponding prediction interval, averaged across simulation runs, and (ii) the mean absolute error (MAE) of coverage relative to the target coverage level. The MAE metric is defined as

$$
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{G} \sum_{g=1}^{G} \left| \hat{c}_g - (1 - \alpha) \right|,
$$

where $\hat{c}_g$ denotes empirical coverage in group $g$, and $G$ is the number of groups or bins under consideration. Lower MAE values indicate more uniform and locally valid coverage. The MAE is computed for each simulation iteration and then averaged across all runs to summarize performance.

In addition to the empirical coverage, we also evaluate the methods for generating prediction intervals using the interval score, using the same setup as in [Appendix A](#appendix-a).

## Aggregate coverage simulations {-}

The first set of simulations evaluates aggregate coverage, averaging across all observations in the test set without conditioning on subgroups or outcome ranges. For each simulation iteration, the data are randomly split into calibration and test sets, and prediction intervals are constructed using SCP, parametric prediction intervals, and bootstrap-based intervals. Here, we compare the SCP method against parametric intervals assuming normal distribution of errors, as well as bootstrapped intervals.

The results, in the table below, show that all three methods achieve nominal coverage very close to the nominal level of 0.9, with MAE values below 0.01. Overall, the differences between the methods are small although there is a minimal tendency towards overcoverage for the normal prediction intervals and towards undercoverage for the bootstrapped intervals.

| Method    | Mean coverage | MAE coverage |
|:----------|:-------------:|:------------:|
| Normal    | 0.902         | 0.005        |
| SCP       | 0.899         | 0.006        |
| Bootstrap | 0.896         | 0.007        |

Table: Aggregate coverage simulation results.

## Subgroup-wise coverage simulations {-}

The second set of simulations evaluates coverage within predefined subgroups of the data. These tests are motivated by the concern that methods with correct aggregate coverage may still exhibit systematic under- or over-coverage within substantively meaningful groups. In each simulation run, prediction intervals are constructed using SCP, MCP, CCP, and DWCP, as well as bootstrapped and parametric (normal) intervals.

Group membership is defined using geographic classifications, corresponding to US Census regions and divisions, as described in the main text. Coverage is computed separately within each group, while MAE of coverage is calculated across groups to quantify uniformity.

The results, in the table below, show that while all methods achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal level in aggregate, the group-aware CP methods (MCP, CCP) have group-wise coverage much closer to the nominal level compared to SCP, bootstrapped, and parametric intervals. In addition, these methods exhibit substantially lower MAE of coverage across regions compared to SCP, bootstrapped, and parametric intervals. This indicates that the group-aware methods provide more uniform and reliable coverage within subpopulations, addressing potential heterogeneity in the data.

| Method    | Midwest | Northeast | South | West  | Mean coverage | MAE coverage |
|:----------|:-------:|:---------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------------:|:------------:|
| MCP       | 0.899   | 0.891     | 0.898 | 0.895 | 0.897         | 0.015        |
| CCP       | 0.899   | 0.886     | 0.900 | 0.882 | 0.896         | 0.016        |
| DWCP      | 0.916   | 0.818     | 0.890 | 0.896 | 0.895         | 0.031        |
| Normal    | 0.927   | 0.826     | 0.901 | 0.879 | 0.902         | 0.032        |
| Bootstrap | 0.924   | 0.825     | 0.891 | 0.877 | 0.896         | 0.033        |
| SCP       | 0.925   | 0.823     | 0.898 | 0.877 | 0.899         | 0.033        |

Table: Subgroup-wise coverage simulation results.

## Coverage within ranges of the target simulations {-}

The third set of simulations focuses on coverage within different ranges of the outcome variable. This scenario is particularly relevant when prediction errors vary systematically across the outcome space, such as in the tails of the distribution. In each simulation iteration, the calibration data are partitioned into bins based on the observed outcome, using thresholds chosen to approximately balance the number of observations across four bins. Prediction intervals are then constructed using BCCP, with both contiguized and non-contiguized variants, alongside standard conformal, parametric, and bootstrap-based intervals. Coverage is then computed separately within each outcome bin. As in the grouped simulations, performance is summarized using mean aggregate coverage and the MAE of bin-wise coverage relative to the nominal level.

The results, in the table below, indicate that both contiguized and non-contiguized BCCP achieve empirical coverage closer to the nominal level within each outcome bin compared to SCP, bootstrapped, and parametric prediction intervals. The MAE of coverage across bins is lowest for the non-contiguized BCCP method, followed by the contiguized version. Both of the BCCP methods have substantially lower MAE across the bins, compared to the alternatives. These findings highlight the effectiveness of BCCP in addressing heterogeneity in prediction errors across the outcome space, leading to more reliable uncertainty quantification. As expected, the aggregate coverage for the contiguized BCCP is moderately higher than nominal due to the effect of contiguization.

| Method    | Bin 1 | Bin 2 | Bin 3 | Bin 4 | Mean coverage | MAE coverage |
|:----------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------------:|:------------:|
| BCCP(d)   | 0.898 | 0.899 | 0.899 | 0.899 | 0.899         | 0.012        |
| BCCP(c)   | 0.898 | 0.967 | 0.928 | 0.899 | 0.924         | 0.030        |
| Normal    | 0.817 | 0.986 | 0.964 | 0.842 | 0.902         | 0.073        |
| SCP       | 0.812 | 0.985 | 0.963 | 0.839 | 0.899         | 0.074        |
| Bootstrap | 0.797 | 0.983 | 0.962 | 0.842 | 0.896         | 0.077        |

Table: Coverage within ranges of the target simulation results.

## Interval score comparison {-}

In addition to empirical coverage, we evaluate the same simulated prediction intervals using the interval score (defined in [Appendix A](#appendix-a)). Lower values indicate sharper and better-calibrated intervals. The reported values are averages over test observations and across the 1000 simulation iterations, computed with the `interval_score()` function.

The tables below report the aggregate interval score, the interval score by US Census region, and the interval score within ranges of the outcome variable.

The results confirm the findings from [Appendix A](#appendix-a), indicating that the group-aware versions of the CP algorithm generally outperform the aggregated versions when comparing the mean interval score across geographic groups. Similarly in agreement with the results from [Appendix A](#appendix-a), the BCCP methods outperform the alternatives on the interval score in the tail-end bins (bin 1 and 4), but underperform in the middle of the distribution.

| Method    | Mean interval score |
|:----------|:-------------------:|
| SCP       | 0.384               |
| Normal    | 0.384               |
| Bootstrap | 0.385               |

Table: Aggregate interval score simulation results. Lower values are better.

| Method    | Midwest | Northeast | South | West  | Mean interval score |
|:----------|:-------:|:---------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------------------:|
| CCP       | 0.357   | 0.357     | 0.377 | 0.395 | 0.371               |
| MCP       | 0.357   | 0.450     | 0.382 | 0.402 | 0.397               |
| DWCP      | 0.358   | 0.480     | 0.376 | 0.401 | 0.404               |
| Normal    | 0.360   | 0.481     | 0.381 | 0.405 | 0.407               |
| SCP       | 0.359   | 0.482     | 0.381 | 0.405 | 0.407               |
| Bootstrap | 0.359   | 0.479     | 0.385 | 0.404 | 0.407               |

Table: Subgroup-wise interval score simulation results by US Census region. Lower values are better.

| Method    | Bin 1 | Bin 2 | Bin 3 | Bin 4 | Mean interval score |
|:----------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------------------:|
| SCP       | 0.438 | 0.318 | 0.327 | 0.447 | 0.382               |
| Normal    | 0.437 | 0.320 | 0.328 | 0.445 | 0.383               |
| Bootstrap | 0.450 | 0.318 | 0.326 | 0.443 | 0.384               |
| BCCP(d)   | 0.420 | 0.369 | 0.375 | 0.399 | 0.391               |
